pathSubtitle: Communicate health concerns, describe symptoms, and understand medical advice clearly.

lessons.title: Describing Basic Symptoms
lessons.situation: You are not feeling well and visit a doctor for the first time.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Hello. Come in and have a seat. What brings you in today?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Hello. I don't feel well. I have a headache and a sore throat.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: I see. How long have you had these symptoms?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: About three days.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Do you have a temperature?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Yes, a little. And I feel very tired.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Let me take a look. Open your mouth, please.

words.definition: a sign of illness felt by a patient
words.example: A sore throat is a common symptom of a cold.

words.definition: a painful or irritated feeling in the throat
words.example: I have a bad sore throat and can't swallow.

words.definition: a pain inside the head
words.example: I've had a headache all day.

words.definition: body heat; a fever when above normal
words.example: The doctor checked my temperature.

words.definition: feeling a need to rest or sleep
words.example: I feel so tired I can barely stand.

lessons.title: Getting a Prescription
lessons.situation: The doctor has examined you and is explaining the diagnosis and treatment.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Based on my examination, you have a throat infection. It's bacterial, so I'm going to prescribe antibiotics.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: How many times a day should I take them?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Twice a day — morning and evening — with food. It's important to finish the full course even if you feel better before then.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Are there any side effects I should know about?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Some people feel nauseous in the first day or two. If you get a rash or have difficulty breathing, stop taking them and come back immediately.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Understood. Is there anything else I can do to help with the pain?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Paracetamol for the pain, plenty of water, and rest. You should feel much better within five days.

words.definition: to officially tell a patient to take a medicine
words.example: The doctor prescribed antibiotics for the infection.

words.definition: medicines that kill bacterial infections
words.example: Always finish your course of antibiotics.

words.definition: an unwanted result of taking a medication
words.example: One side effect of this medicine is dizziness.

words.definition: feeling like you want to vomit
words.example: The medicine made me feel nauseous.

words.definition: the full set of doses of a medicine
words.example: Complete the full course of medication.

lessons.title: Describing Pain
lessons.situation: You are visiting a doctor for back pain and need to describe it accurately.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Where exactly does it hurt?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: In my lower back, on the right side. It started after I moved some heavy boxes last week.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: And how would you describe the pain? Is it sharp, dull, burning?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: It's more of a dull, constant ache. But when I bend down, it becomes quite sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: On a scale of one to ten, how bad is the pain right now?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: About a five or six at rest, but an eight when I move.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Does it radiate anywhere — down your leg, for example?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Sometimes. I get a tingling feeling down the back of my right leg.

words.definition: a sudden, intense pain (like a knife)
words.example: I feel a sharp pain when I breathe in.

words.definition: a continuous, low-level pain that is not intense
words.example: I have a dull ache in my shoulder.

words.definition: happening all the time without stopping
words.example: The pain is constant — it never goes away.

words.definition: to spread out from a central point
words.example: The pain radiates from my back to my leg.

words.definition: a light prickling sensation in the skin
words.example: I have a tingling feeling in my fingers.

lessons.title: Mental Health Consultation
lessons.situation: You visit your GP to discuss how you have been feeling mentally and emotionally.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: You mentioned on the form that you've been feeling low. Can you tell me more about that?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: Over the past couple of months, I haven't been sleeping well, and I've lost interest in things I used to enjoy. I feel exhausted most of the time, even when I haven't done much.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or feeling like life isn't worth living?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: No, nothing like that. It's more like a persistent grey feeling — not acute sadness, just flatness.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: That sounds like it could be depression, though we'd want to rule out physical causes first. How is your appetite, and have you had any significant life changes recently?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: My appetite is down. And yes — I changed jobs six months ago and it's been more stressful than I expected.

words.definition: extremely tired, with no energy left
words.example: I feel completely exhausted, even after a full night's sleep.

words.definition: continuing for a long time; not stopping
words.example: She has a persistent cough that won't go away.

words.definition: severe and sudden in onset (in medical terms)
words.example: The patient arrived with acute chest pain.

words.definition: to eliminate something as a possibility
words.example: We need to rule out any physical causes first.

words.definition: the natural desire to eat food
words.example: I've had no appetite this week.

lessons.title: Specialist Referral & Second Opinion
lessons.situation: Your GP is referring you to a specialist. You ask informed questions about the referral process.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Based on your test results, I'd like to refer you to a cardiologist. Your ECG shows some irregularities that warrant further investigation.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I see. Can you explain what kind of irregularities we're talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: There are some anomalies in your heart rhythm — nothing that points definitively to a serious condition, but we shouldn't ignore them.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: How long is the waiting time for a referral, typically?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Under the NHS, it should be within 18 weeks. However, given the nature of the findings, I'll mark it as urgent, which should accelerate that considerably.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.text: I'd also like to consider seeking a private second opinion. Is that something you'd advise against?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.text: Not at all. A second opinion is your right, and for anything cardiac-related, it's entirely reasonable. I can provide you with a full summary of your results.

words.definition: when a doctor sends a patient to see a specialist
words.example: I have a referral to see a specialist next month.

words.definition: a doctor who specialises in the heart
words.example: The cardiologist reviewed my ECG results.

words.definition: something that is irregular or unexpected
words.example: The scan revealed a small anomaly.

words.definition: asking another doctor to confirm or review a diagnosis
words.example: I decided to get a second opinion before the operation.

words.definition: relating to the heart
words.example: He is in the cardiac care unit.
